name: Electrical and Computer Engineering
notes: 128 total credits: 52 core, 12 advanced electives and design, 16 math, 12 science, 12 cluster, 8 humanities/social science, 6 primary and upper-level writing, 10 elective.

Writing is satisfied by WRTG 105 (primary), WRTG 273 (2 credits, typically second year), and the writing embedded in third- and fourth-year ECE core courses with laboratory components (ECE 216, 221, 222, 230). WRTG 273 is modeled as the ULW requirement.

The humanities/social science requirement is five courses (20 credits) INCLUDING the three-course cluster, so two further H/SS courses are required beyond the cluster. Language courses at the 101 level count only when followed by a more advanced course in the same language. A minor of five or more courses in one area also satisfies it.
PHYS 113 is an acceptable replacement for PHYS 121 only for students taking the MATH 141-143 calculus sequence - not modeled as an alternative.

The three advanced electives may be concentrated in one area (Computer Engineering, Semiconductor Devices, Integrated Circuits, Waves and Fields, Signals/Communication/Image Processing, Robotics) or spread for breadth. Other upper-level courses may be approved by the undergraduate chair.

name: Engineering and Applied Sciences
notes: IMPORTANT - this is an INDIVIDUALLY DESIGNED major. The page states plainly: 'The program approved by the committee for a given student constitutes that student's degree requirements.' There is no fixed course list. What follows models the structural rules the page gives (how many courses in each area), NOT a specific approved program. Your own approved proposal is the authority.

Students devise the major from the offerings of two or more engineering departments, and must submit the proposed program to the Engineering and Applied Sciences Program Committee, which may accept, reject, or require modification.

Natural sciences: eight courses - three mathematics including one in differential equations, four in physics or chemistry with at least one of each, and one additional mathematics or natural science course. Modeled as counts; the differential-equations and one-of-each constraints are not auto-enforced.

Core: at least eight 4-credit engineering courses from two or more departments, at least half at the 200 level. May include the upper-level writing and computational analysis courses. Up to eight credit hours of independent study may be included. The two-or-more-departments rule is not auto-enforced.

Technical sequences: three sequences of at least three courses each, with no more than one introductory-level course per sequence, where a sequence is 'a logical progression of study, confined to an acceptably identifiable area, in which later material builds upon and extends earlier material.' These nine courses overlap with the core if the student wishes, so they are NOT modeled as an additional nine-course block - doing so would roughly double the real requirement.
The senior design project EAS 393 may be replaced with pre-approval by a departmental senior design sequence (AME 386+387, BME 296, CHE 255, ECE 348+349, ME 204+205, OPT 310+311).

name: Chemistry

Senior research is two semesters totalling eight credits of CHEM 393, plus a written thesis read and approved by the research advisor and a second chemistry faculty member. The app places CHEM 393 once; the second semester is not separately represented.

name: Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences
notes: This is the department's current BS, replacing the retired BS in Environmental Science (EVS), which is no longer offered to new students and is deliberately absent from this app.
19 courses total, with a choice of three tracks: Climate and Environmental Sciences, Geosciences, or Earth and Planetary Sciences.

The three tracks differ in how their 19 courses are apportioned (Climate: 4 advanced core + 4 technical electives; Geosciences: 4 advanced core + 3 technical electives; Earth and Planetary: 3 advanced core + 5 technical electives). The Geosciences track additionally requires four one-credit 200-level labs, at least three from EES Department courses. Lab components are marked (L) on the page and are not separately modeled.

AP credit is acceptable for the supporting science and math courses upon approval.

name: International Political Analysis (IPA)
notes: DELIBERATELY NOT ENCODED - no verifiable source exists. name: Political Science
notes: Requirements apply to the Class of 2021 and later; earlier classes may follow the old requirements, which are not modeled.

name: Audio Arts and Technology
notes: The AAT BA requires 54 credit hours in the major, including a two-credit upper-level writing course. This is the BA in Audio Arts and Technology - a different degree from the BS in Audio and Music Engineering (major-ame-bs).
CLUSTERS ARE SPECIFIED: two clusters, one in the humanities and one in a social science.
PRIMARY WRITING: all students must complete WRTG 105 or its equivalent.
MATH 171 or MATH 141 can substitute for MATH 161 depending on placement by the Department of Mathematics.
The programming requirement may also be satisfied with CSC 161, but students should contact the AME 262/AME 264 instructor to demonstrate familiarity with C and C++ before taking those courses.
AME 385 (the capstone) requires instructor permission to register; the advisor you choose depends on your project proposal, and the project is typically completed in the senior year.
The program is deliberately flexible so students can combine it with music, business and economics, media studies, studio arts, English and film studies, biology, psychology or other areas.
For more detail see the AAT Curriculum Guide (PDF) linked from the department page - it is not part of this snapshot.
Group sizes here follow the page's own course counts (four AME electives, two arts-and-science electives); the page states the credit total as 54 rather than listing credits per group.

name: Classical Civilization
notes: Eleven courses: one foundation course, three subject courses (one from each subject group), two concentration courses in a single subject area, four electives, and the senior capstone.
This is a different major from Classics (major-clst-ba), which requires Greek or Latin language work.

Some courses overlap categories - for example Ancient Greek and Roman Historiography (CLST 220) may satisfy either the History or the Literature requirement, but not both. The groups below do not share courses, which matches that rule.

The literature subject group also admits any LATN or CGRK course at the 200 level or above; those are not enumerable as a fixed list here, so the literature group lists only the CLST courses the page names.

CONCENTRATION COURSES - NEEDS VERIFICATION: two additional courses both drawn from ONE of the three subject areas, determined with the major advisor, at least one at the 200 level. The planner cannot enforce 'both from the same area', so the group below accepts any two subject-area courses with at least one at the 200 level. Confirm your pair with your advisor.

CAPSTONE: the capstone experience is a four-credit course or equivalent with a significant writing component, built on an area of strength already demonstrated through coursework - it is proposed by the student rather than being a fixed course. Only the accompanying one-credit Senior Capstone Workshop (CLST 389) is a fixed course code, so it is what the capstone group checks. Work in the two concentration courses should ideally feed the capstone.

NEEDS VERIFICATION: several course numbers the page lists (CLST 123, 130, 132, 160, 232, 234, 265, 290, 291, 292, and CLST 167a/167b which the catalog carries as CLST 167M) are absent from the 2025-26 catalog under those numbers. They are kept as options because the page names them.

name: Digital Media Studies
notes: Digital Media Studies is a 14-course interdisciplinary major: four introductory courses, four technology/production courses, three media history/theory/practice courses, one digital-applications course, and the two-course capstone.

Students choose their divisional area when they declare their major. Seven of a DMS major's fourteen courses must be in the divisional area they declare.' This entry is filed under humanities; if you declare natural science, the cluster requirement shifts accordingly. The page marks each course (H), (NS) or (SS) - the planner does not track the seven-course divisional split, so count it yourself.
Students must complete at least two of the four core courses before they can declare the major. The core courses are offered both fall and spring and need not be taken consecutively.

CAPSTONE PREREQUISITES: DMST 103 must be completed by the end of sophomore year and DMST 200W by the end of junior year; the capstone itself runs the full senior year (DMST 372 fall, DMST 373 spring).
Technology/production should total 16 credit hours - if you choose a 2-credit course from that list (EAS 141, ME 110), pair it with another 2-credit course.

Courses appearing in BOTH the technology/production and media history/theory/practice lists may count toward either component, but not both. The groups below do not share courses, which matches that rule.

ART NEW YORK: two of the three courses in the Art New York internship sequence count toward the major - SART 300 (Art New York New Field Studio) toward technology/production and SART 301 (Art New York Colloquium) toward media history/theory/practice. Permission from the DMS program director is required, and the upper-level writing designation depends on the nature of the student's project.
HIST 246 and HIST 285 are upper-level-writing qualified and may substitute for the ULW course in the media history/theory/practice component - but you must register for the W section.

name: Interdepartmental Studies
notes: AN INDIVIDUALLY DESIGNED MAJOR. Only the structural counts the College publishes are modeled - ten core courses from at least two departments, plus up to four optional supplementary courses. The specific courses are whatever the student's own proposal names, approved by the Committee on Individualized Interdepartmental Programs (CIIP) and supervised by two faculty advisors. The approved proposal, not this entry, is the student's actual degree requirement.

This is the School of Arts & Sciences side of the University's interdepartmental degree program. The Hajim School equivalent is the BS in Engineering and Applied Sciences (major-eas-bs), which is a separate entry.
The only degree option for this program is a bachelor of arts.
'AT LEAST TWO DEPARTMENTS' IS NOT ENFORCED: the core group below accepts ten courses from anywhere in the catalog, because the departments differ with every proposal. Check the spread yourself.

AUTO-GENERATE IS NOT USEFUL HERE: because the ten core courses may come from any department, the generator will fill them with ten arbitrary four-credit courses. Place the courses from your approved proposal yourself and use this entry to track the count. Generation is also slow for the same reason - the scheduler scores the whole catalog.
The four supplementary courses are optional (the page says 'up to four'), so they are not modeled as a requirement group.

APPLY EARLY: 'Because individualized majors require more time to organize than traditional majors or minors, interested students should begin their preparation as early as possible. Students can apply up until second semester of their junior year.' Beginning in fall 2021 seniors are not eligible to apply, and beginning in fall 2024 proposals for interdepartmental MINORS are no longer accepted.

Ask yourself first whether some combination of existing majors, minors or certificates would serve - an interdepartmental proposal is for interests that existing programs cannot meet. Degrees or minors of a pre-professional nature (for example pre-med or physical therapy) cannot be approved.

DEADLINES: the Interdepartmental Faculty Recommender Agreement Form (one per faculty advisor, two advisors required) is due October 1 for the fall semester or March 1 for the spring; the full application - proposal form, proposal essays and faculty recommendation forms - is due October 15 or March 15. Incomplete proposals are not reviewed.
Amy Fisher is the interdepartmental studies program advisor and the contact point for all forms.
Interdepartmental clusters (cluster IDs containing 'INT') remain available through the cluster search engine.

DIVISION IS DETERMINED BY YOUR COURSEWORK: 'To achieve a degree in the chosen division (humanities or social sciences), students must have completed at least 24 credit hours in the designated division, at least 12 of which (3 courses) must be a mid- or upper-level course in that division.' INTERDISCIPLINARY SPREAD IS NOT ENFORCED: 'Students must take courses from at least three different departments or programs, and mid- and upper-level courses from at least two different departments.' Check that spread yourself.

GEOGRAPHIC BREADTH IS NOT FULLY ENFORCED: the rule is at least one course in TWO of the three geographies (Caribbean, mainland Latin America, U.S. Latinx diaspora). The group below asks for two courses from the combined list, so make sure yours fall in two different geographies.

name: Music
notes: The Arthur Satz Department of Music, in cooperation with the Eastman School of Music, offers the BA in music. Requirements are stated in credits; the groups below convert them to course counts.

EMPHASES ARE NOT MODELED SEPARATELY. Every music major picks one of nine emphases - Basic, Composition, History/Theory, Music in World Cultures, Musical Theater, Performance, Popular Music/Jazz, Audio and Music Engineering, or Conducting. The page states these 'are not separate degrees and will not appear on the diploma'; all of them share the core requirements and differ only in how many semesters of lessons and ensembles they need and what the electives must be. This entry encodes the CORE plus the BASIC EMPHASIS (63 credits: four semesters of studio lessons, four semesters of ensemble, eight elective credits). Check your emphasis' own line in the department's degree-requirements PDF.

Non-basic emphases at a glance: Composition 67 cr (12 credits of composition/theory electives); History/Theory 63 cr (2 semesters of lessons, 12 credits of history/theory electives); Music in World Cultures 63 cr (2 semesters of lessons, 2 semesters of world-music ensemble, MUSC 121 and MUSC 280, 4 elective credits of world music - and its 'Music in World Cultures' core course must be MUSC 210 or MUSC 236, not MUSC 121); Musical Theater 65 cr (4 semesters of studio voice, MUSC 133 and MUSC 163, 4 elective credits); Performance 73 cr (6 semesters/16 credits of lessons, 6 semesters of ensemble); Popular Music/Jazz 63 cr (12 elective credits in popular music); Audio and Music Engineering 63 cr (12 elective credits in audio and music engineering); Conducting 65 cr (Introduction to the Art of Conducting plus independent study as assistant conductor).

NOT MODELED - PRIVATE INSTRUCTION: the basic emphasis requires four semesters of studio lessons at Eastman or on the carillon. Eastman studio-lesson courses are not in the AS&E catalog, so the planner cannot track them. No more than 8 credits of private instruction count toward the degree (the performance emphasis excepted).

ENSEMBLES REPEAT: the requirement is four SEMESTERS of ensemble participation, which is usually the same ensemble taken repeatedly. The planner counts distinct courses, so the ensemble group asks for four different ensemble course codes; in practice repeating one ensemble four times satisfies the department. No more than 8 ensemble credits count toward the degree (the performance emphasis excepted). MUSC 155 (Chamber Ensembles), MUSC 157A (Jazz Combos) and MUSC 165 (Mbira Ensemble) explicitly do NOT count toward the ensemble requirement.

PLACEMENT: students who do not qualify for MUSC 111 enroll in MUSC 110 (Introduction to Music Theory) first; the theory placement exam is given during summer orientation. Musicianship normally starts at MUSC 113, but the supervising faculty member may direct a student to start elsewhere, and MUSC 109 is added if needed - hence the stated 2-4 credit range for musicianship.
Keyboard skills may also be satisfied by passing an equivalent proficiency exam for each of MUSC 116 and MUSC 117.
In accordance with University policy, no more than 80 credit hours can be taken in a student's concentration.

name: Russian Studies
notes: Russian Studies is an interdisciplinary program drawing on three core departments - Modern Languages and Cultures, History, and Political Science - and is a DIFFERENT major from Russian (major-russ-ba), which is the MLC language-and-literature major. Its coursework also includes courses in or cross-listed with religion and classics, Judaic studies, Polish and Central European studies, film studies, gender/sexuality and women's studies, comparative literature, art and art history, and economics.
The major has ten required courses in total.

DIVISION IS THE STUDENT'S CHOICE: 'The Russian studies major and minor can be counted in either humanities or social sciences, depending on your choice of courses (to count as social science, the majority of courses must be taken in history, international relations and political science).' This entry is filed under humanities; if the majority of your courses are history/IR/political science it counts as social science instead and your cluster requirement shifts accordingly.

COURSE LISTS ARE NOT PUBLISHED ON THIS PAGE - NEEDS VERIFICATION: the page states the CATEGORIES (Russian literature, Russian history, political science) but points to a separate 'complete list of Russian courses' PDF for the actual courses, which is not part of this snapshot. The groups below therefore accept any RUSS course, any HIST course and any PSCI course respectively. That is looser than the real requirement: your history and political-science courses must have a Russian, Eurasian or international-relations focus, and your RUSS courses must be literature rather than language. Check every choice against the department PDF or with a Russian advisor - the planner cannot tell a Russia-focused history course from any other.

PROFICIENCY IN RUSSIAN: coursework through RUSS 152 (Intermediate Russian II), or approved equivalent coursework. Earlier RUSS language courses are prerequisites to it rather than separate requirements. Placement is by online exam; students with no previous Russian may register for RUSS 101 without one.

SENIOR THESIS - NEEDS VERIFICATION: the page lists a senior thesis among the two-to-three foundation courses but gives it no course number, and the catalog has no RUSS thesis course. The MLC research seminar CLTR 389 and honors thesis CLTR 393H are the department's nearest thesis-bearing courses and are offered as the options here; confirm the right registration with the program director.

STUDY ABROAD: students can study Russian in Estonia, Armenia or Kazakhstan for a summer or a semester through American Councils or CIEE. Ask a Russian advisor how courses taken abroad count toward the major.
There is also a Russian Studies cluster in each of the humanities and social-science divisions (H1RST005 for humanities).

No more than two transferred studio courses are accepted toward the major.

Majors must present a senior exhibition (SART 399) with a defense; documentation is retained by the department. The exhibition is not modeled as one of the twelve courses.
Honors requires a 3.5 GPA within the major - not modeled.

name: Theater
notes: A special major offered by the English department in conjunction with the University's International Theatre Program. All of its courses carry ENGL numbers - the THTR numbers introduced for summer 2026 are not used by this page and are not in the 2025-26 catalog.
A minimum of ten courses (at least 40 credit hours) in English and theater are required.

The page lists spring-semester course numbers in parentheses beside the fall numbers (for example ENGL 184 in fall, ENGL 185 in spring). Both numbers of each pair are listed as options here; several of the spring numbers (ENGL 155, 171, 175, 179, 185) do not appear in the 2025-26 catalog.

NOT A COURSE REQUIREMENT: within the sixteen production credits, each student must work on at least four productions and serve in stage management or as an assistant director for at least one of them.

In cases where some courses are unavailable, students should consult the director of undergraduate studies for possible substitutions. Other courses in the English department relating to drama and/or theater may from time to time be valid additions to the method/performance list, and ENGL 398 (Internship in Theater), ENGL 391 (Independent Study), ENGL 380 (Advanced Seminar) or ENGL 396 (Honors Seminar) with a dramatic-literature or theatrical focus might also count. Study abroad in London and Bath focused on dramatic or theatrical work may also count.
Students wanting a dramatic-literature course outside the listed five must get the program director's approval in advance of registering.

NEEDS VERIFICATION - UPPER-LEVEL WRITING: the page states no ULW policy for this major, and the 2025-26 catalog contains no W-suffixed ENGL courses at the 200-399 level, so none is encoded. Confirm with the director of undergraduate studies how you will satisfy the College ULW requirement.
ENGL 154/155 (Intro to Design for the Stage) is a 2-credit course, so a student who uses it toward the eight method/performance credits needs a third course in that category.

requirementGroups.label: One literature survey course
requirementGroups.sourceQuote: One Survey Course. Students must take one of the following: ENGL 112: Classical and Scriptural Backgrounds; ENGL 113: British Literature I; ENGL 114: British Literature II; ENGL 115: American Literature; ENGL 116: Intro to African American Literature

requirementGroups.label: Sixteen credit hours in theater production
requirementGroups.sourceQuote: Sixteen Credit Hours in Theater Production. Sixteen credit hours must be in theater production, either onstage or backstage. Each student must work on at least four productions, serving in stage management or as an assistant director for at least one. Students can choose from the following (Spring course numbers in parentheses): ENGL 184 (185): Intro to Theater; ENGL 292 (293)/ 294 (295): Plays in Performance: Name of Play; ENGL 296 (297): Stage Management
requirementGroups.note: Sixteen credits at 4 credits each = four courses, matching the four productions each student must work on.

requirementGroups.label: Eight credit hours in theater method/performance
requirementGroups.sourceQuote: Eight Credit Hours in Theater Method/Performance. Eight hours of credit must be in theater method and/or performance courses, choosing from the following (Spring course numbers in parentheses): ENGL 123: Playwriting; ENGL 124: Intro to Stage Lighting; ENGL 154 (155): Intro to Design for the Stage - 2 credits; ENGL 156; ENGL 164; ENGL 165; ENGL 170 (171); ENGL 172 (173); ENGL 174 (175); ENGL 176; ENGL 177; ENGL 178 (179); ENGL 180; ENGL 181; ENGL 182; ENGL 252; ENGL 270; ENGL 271; ENGL 272; ENGL 273; ENGL 278; ENGL 279; ENGL 290; ENGL 291; ENGL 360: Special Projects: Theater; Other classes offered occasionally may also fill this requirment

requirementGroups.note: The four pre-1800 options are the medieval, Renaissance, Shakespeare and Restoration/eighteenth-century courses; ENGL 235 covers post-1800 drama.

name: Aerospace Engineering
notes: Four courses. Non-ME majors take three aerospace core courses and one mechanical engineering course; ME majors take all four from the aerospace core list.
Open to all majors and particularly compatible with mechanical engineering, physics, optical engineering, chemical engineering, and electrical and computer engineering.

SENIOR DESIGN: students not taking a senior design course as part of their major must take ME 205 (Advanced Mechanical Design) and complete the aerospace design project in that class. The instructor issues a letter certifying the project - that is also what makes ME 205 count as an aerospace core course.
Up to two courses from the minor can be used toward a separate major or minor - EXCEPT for the mechanical engineering major, which may overlap only one course.
Students cannot declare a minor until accepted into a major, and cannot elect the satisfactory/fail option for minor courses.
Contact Professor John Lambropoulos, who evaluates and manages all ME minors, before declaring.

requirementGroups.label: Three aerospace core courses
requirementGroups.sourceQuote: Aerospace Core Courses. At least three of the following courses*: ME 205: Advanced Mechanical Design**; ME 214/407: Advanced Dynamics; ME 222/424: Introduction to Robust Design and Quality Engineering; ME 227/427: Introduction to Aerodynamics; ME 231/431: Feedback Control of Dynamic Systems; ME 232/432: Opto-Mechanical Design; ME 246/446: Aerospace Structures; ME 254/441: Finite Element Methods. *Mechanical engineering majors must choose all four of their minor courses from this list.

The six courses must include courses from at least two different disciplines - not auto-enforced (BLST courses are cross-listed from many home departments).

BME 211, BME 258, and BME 459 count as LIFE SCIENCE courses and cannot be used for the engineering requirement.
The engineering requirement is 12 credits: eight BME credits plus four additional engineering credits. 400-level BME and cross-listed courses may be included.

name: Chemistry
notes: Any six chemistry courses of four credits or more, totalling at least 24 credit hours.
300-level courses are NOT included. 400-level courses may be included with instructor permission - not modeled.
CHEM 111 Molecules of Power may NOT be used; it is intended for humanities and social science concentrators.
BIOL 250 is no longer an allowed substitute for CHEM 262 for newly created programs of study.

Two courses with substantial overlap of content should not both be included.

requirementGroups.label: Six chemistry courses (24+ credits)

name: Chinese
notes: THE NEW CURRICULUM (effective fall 2026) is encoded: five courses total. The old requirement, in effect through spring 2026, was SIX courses - a three-course language sequence plus three additional courses in Chinese language, culture, literature, art, history or politics.

PLACEMENT EXCEPTIONS: students who place into or above the 205 level may complete the minor with five four-credit courses in Chinese language, literature, culture, art, history or religion. Students placing beyond the 206 level may take no language coursework at all and complete the minor with five content courses.

No more than two courses total may be transferred in from other institutions or taken in non-MLC departments (HIST, ANTH, RELC, AHST and so on). Courses cross-listed with CHIN but parented in another department count as outside courses - except CHIN 215, CHIN 225 and CHIN 238 (parented as JPNS 217, JPNS 225 and JPNS 237), which count as normal CHIN courses.
CHIN 391 (independent study) may count with advisor approval; CHIN 390 (supervised teaching) may not. No two-credit courses count toward the minor - hence the 4-credit floor on both groups.

requirementGroups.label: Chinese language sequence (three courses)

requirementGroups.label: Two Chinese electives

name: Digital Media Studies
notes: Six courses. THE HUMANITIES TRACK IS ENCODED HERE.

The HUMANITIES track needs four of the six courses to be humanities courses (DMST 101 + DMST 103 + at least two more H courses, plus one or two NS courses). The NATURAL SCIENCES track needs four of the six to be natural-science courses: DMST 101 plus DMST 102 or CSC 161, then three NS courses and one H course. If you declare the NS track, read the option lists below in the opposite proportion.
The DMS MAJOR is a separate entry (major-dmst-ba).

name: East Asian Studies
notes: Five courses (three foundational surveys, two electives) and no prerequisites. Designed for students with a strong interest in East Asia who are not planning to learn an East Asian language.

name: Climate Change Science
notes: A minimum of 24 credits (six four-credit courses) are required.

The page states one introductory course and 'at least two' core courses, then lists the upper-level selections without a count; six courses at 4 credits meets the 24-credit floor, so three upper-level courses are modeled. Confirm the split with the department.

Students who complete this minor will understand the natural and anthropogenic causes of climate change, its impacts on physical, chemical and biological processes in the atmosphere and oceans, and how future climate is modeled or past climate measured.
Several of these courses carry substantial prerequisites in mathematics, chemistry and physics - see the source quotes.
See the department's major/minor course overlap policy.

requirementGroups.sourceQuote: Required Courses. One of the following (but not both): EESC 103: Introduction to Environmental Science; EESC 105: Introduction to Climate Change
requirementGroups.note: One of these, but NOT both.

notes: A coherent sequence of 16 credits plus a required background course. Students need a GPA of at least 2.0 to declare.
PREREQUISITES: one semester of chemistry, two semesters of calculus and one semester of physics. AP equivalents or instructor approval are acceptable.
Substitutions the page allows: ME 123 for CHE 225, ME 225 for CHE 243, ME 223 for CHE 244.

requirementGroups.label: Required background

requirementGroups.label: Sixteen credits of environmental engineering coursework
requirementGroups.sourceQuote: Choose 16 Credits. No more than 12 credits can be taken from one department. Students not majoring in engineering should take 12 credits in engineering courses (CHE or ME). Students majoring in engineering should take 12 of the 16 credits in non-engineering courses (EES, BIO, PHLT).
requirementGroups.note: BALANCE RULE NOT ENFORCED: no more than 12 of the 16 credits may come from one department, and the engineering/non-engineering split runs OPPOSITE ways depending on your major - engineering majors take 12 credits OUTSIDE engineering, everyone else takes 12 credits INSIDE it. Check your own split.

name: Epidemiology
notes: Six courses; fulfills the social sciences academic division of the Rochester Curriculum.

name: Geological Sciences

name: German

name: Health, Behavior, and Society

name: Health Policy

NO MORE THAN ONE COURSE may overlap between a public health minor and another program of study.

requirementGroups.sourceQuote: Required Courses. PHLT 101: Introduction to Public Health I; PHLT 116: Introduction to the U.S Health System

name: International Relations

Courses used for tools of political analysis cannot also satisfy the core track or breadth.
The three IR core tracks are Governance of Nations, Peace and Conflict, and Politics/Policy/Development - the same track data the IR major uses.

requirementGroups.label: Core track (3 courses from one track)

requirementGroups.label: Five Japanese language and culture courses

name: Latin American, Caribbean, and Latinx Studies

name: Latin

name: Legal Studies
notes: Six courses. An interdisciplinary minor administered by the philosophy department that examines law from several perspectives. It is NOT pre-professional training, though it should be useful for anyone considering law school.

No more than two courses used for your major(s) may be used toward the minor.
